rationale: Matthew 15:30-31 lists "the lame, the blind, the crippled, the mute" and ends with "the mute speaking, the crippled restored, the lame walking, and the blind seeing" (BSB). Isaiah 35:5-6 promises that "the eyes of the blind will be opened and the ears of the deaf unstopped. Then the lame will leap like a deer" (BSB). Three Greek nouns are shared with the Septuagint of Isaiah 35:5-6: typhlos (blind), kophos and cholos (lame). But kophos means "mute" in Matthew 15:31 (the kophoi are "speaking") and "deaf" in Isaiah 35:5, and none of the verbs match: Matthew's peripatountas and blepontas against the Septuagint's haleitai and anoichthesontai. That holds in the SBL, NA/WH, Byzantine and TR texts; the Greek Orthodox Church 1904 text reads kophous akouontas, alalous lalountas ("the deaf hearing, the mute speaking"), sharing akouo with Isaiah 35:5. The grade stays plausible because that shared verb is in one edition only, and even there the match is one verb with the deaf, without a formula. Gill (via the Biblehub aggregator) says these cures were "as was prophesied of the times of the Messiah" and cites Isaiah 35:5, without further argument. Graded plausible, following conn-matt9-blind-isaiah35, and below conn-matt11-blind-isaiah35 (strong), whose 11:5 matches three groups and one full verb-noun pairing. Matthew uses no formula here. Mark's account of the same journey has one healing, of a man "deaf and hardly able to speak" (Mark 7:32, BSB); Meyer notes that Mark's word for him, mogilalon, is the Septuagint's word in Isaiah 35:6 (a reading of Mark, not of Matthew).
